title: NLRB v. Wyman-Gordon Co. (1969)
summary: An agency may not make a prospective rule of general application in an adjudication while skipping the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking requirements, but an order issued to a party in its own adjudication remains enforceable.
notes:
Key line: The rule-making provisions of that Act, which the Board would avoid, were designed to assure fairness and mature consideration of rules of general application. (Justice Fortas, plurality)

Citation: 394 U.S. 759 (1969).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was the National Labor Relations Board. The respondent was Wyman-Gordon Company, a manufacturer whose employees were the subject of a representation election sought by two unions, the United Steelworkers of America and the International Brotherhood of Boilermakers. Solicitor General Erwin Griswold argued for the Board; the AFL-CIO filed an amicus brief supporting it. The case turned on the status of the requirement announced in the Board's earlier decision in Excelsior Underwear Inc., 156 N.L.R.B. 1236 (1966), that employers furnish lists of eligible voters before elections.
sections.Material Facts: In Excelsior Underwear, decided in 1966 after the Board invited briefs from interested parties, the Board announced in an adjudication that employers must file within seven days after an election is directed a list of names and addresses of eligible voters. The Board did not apply the requirement to the parties in Excelsior; it stated the rule would govern only elections directed thirty days or more after the decision. The Board never used the notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures of the Administrative Procedure Act. In this case the Board ordered a representation election among Wyman-Gordon's employees and directed the company to furnish a list of eligible employees. The company refused. The election was held without the list and both unions lost. The Board set the election aside and ordered a new one; the company again refused to supply the list. The Board issued a subpoena for the list, and the company refused to comply.
sections.Procedural History: The Board filed an action in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts to enforce its subpoena or, alternatively, for an injunction compelling compliance with its order. The District Court held the Board's order valid and directed the company to comply. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed, holding the order invalid because it rested on the Excelsior rule, which had not been promulgated in accordance with the APA's rulemaking requirements, 397 F.2d 394 (1968). The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on March 3, 1969, and decided the case on April 23, 1969. It reversed and remanded with directions to reinstate the District Court's judgment. Justice Fortas announced the judgment and wrote for four Justices.
sections.Issue: Was the Excelsior requirement, announced in an adjudication but applied only prospectively to future elections and never to the parties before the Board, a valid rule despite the Board's failure to use the notice-and-comment procedures of section 4 of the Administrative Procedure Act? If the Excelsior rule was invalid, could the Board nevertheless enforce, by subpoena or injunction, the order it issued to Wyman-Gordon in this adjudicatory proceeding directing the company to furnish the list of eligible employees? Was such a list evidence within the meaning of section 11 of the National Labor Relations Act so that a subpoena could reach it?
sections.Holding: The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed. Justice Fortas, for four Justices, concluded that in Excelsior the Board purported to exercise quasi-legislative power and to make a rule without following the APA's rulemaking requirements, so the Excelsior rule is invalid; but in this case the company was directed in an adjudicatory proceeding to submit the list, that order was within the Board's substantive authority and reasonable, and it was the order, not the Excelsior rule, that the company was bound to obey. The list is evidence subject to subpoena under section 11. Three Justices concurred in the result on the ground that Excelsior itself was valid adjudication. The District Court's judgment enforcing the order is reinstated.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Fortas wrote that the APA's rulemaking provisions were designed to assure fairness and mature consideration of rules of general application and may not be avoided by making rules in the course of adjudication. Adjudicated cases may serve as vehicles for announcing agency policy, and such policy may guide later cases, but in Excelsior the Board did not adjudicate: it declined to apply its new requirement to the parties before it and instead announced a rule for the future, which is legislative action requiring the APA's procedures of notice, comment and publication. Even so, Fortas found no reason to deny enforcement of the Board's order here. The Board in this proceeding directed the company to furnish the list. That direction fell within the Board's wide discretion to ensure fair and free elections, because giving unions the names and addresses of voters furthers informed choice. The Board might have reached its decision by relying on Excelsior as a precedent stated in an adjudication, and it committed no error by applying a requirement the Board could lawfully impose case by case. Fortas rejected the argument that the Board's explicit reliance on the invalid rule required a remand under SEC v. Chenery, since the Board's decision was one it was plainly entitled to make on the record. Finally, names and addresses in the company's records are evidence relevant to the Board's election proceedings, so section 11 authorized the subpoena.

topics.lrs-o-chenery-reasons: The narrow futility discussion contrasts an uncontestable command with Chenery’s unresolved discretionary judgment; the fractured opinions require careful attribution.
topics.lrs-o-retroactivity: Fortas questioned the general future-only Excelsior policy; Black defended adjudicatory development of policy. These are different rationales, not an agreed majority rule.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: The plurality treated Excelsior's prospective roster requirement as a rule that should have gone through § 553 procedures.

learning.separateOpinions: Six to three on the judgment, with no majority rationale. Justice Black, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall, concurred in the result, reasoning that Excelsior was a legitimate adjudication, that the choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies in the Board's informed discretion, and that a prospective application did not make the decision any less adjudicatory. Justice Douglas dissented, insisting that a rule of this kind must go through APA rulemaking and that the Board's order could not be sustained. Justice Harlan dissented, agreeing with the plurality that Excelsior was invalid rulemaking but concluding that because the Board relied on that rule the order must be set aside and the Board required to proceed properly.
